list-item.p: ASRT enables fast online MRIgRT fast adaptation for thoracic tumors.
ASRT corrects daily ED and body contour changes impacting dose distribution.
ASRT improved target coverage with no changes in organs at risk.
No grade ≥ 3 toxicities observed; grade 2 in only 10.3% of patients.
1-year local control, DFS, and OS were 94%, 80%, and 84%, respectively.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The thorax presents unique challenges in radiotherapy: although stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) achieves high local control in NSCLC and pulmonary metastases, further improvements are desirable, particularly dose escalation in radioresistant metastases and planning target volume (PTV) margin reduction to minimize toxicity. Online adaptive Magnetic Resonance Imaging-guided Radiotherapy (MRIgART) supports these strategies by ensuring daily dose accuracy through compensation of Electron Density (ED) variations. However, prolonged treatment times remain the main obstacle to clinical implementation. To address this limitation, we introduce Adaptive Skin Radiotherapy (ASRT), a time-efficient MRIgART workflow designed to maintain accuracy while enhancing feasibility.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Lung patients undergoing MRIgART were prospectively enrolled and treated with a biologically effective dose (BED) higher than 100 Gy. The gross tumor volume (GTV) was delineated on a simulation MRI co-registered with the staging CT, and the planning target volume (PTV) was generated by isotropically expanding the GTV by 3 mm. Gross tumor volume (GTV) was delineated on simulation MRI co-registered with staging CT, and planning target volume (PTV) was created by isotropically expanding GTV by 3 mm. ASRT involves a rapid online workflow where only body contour and target are recontoured, minimizing changes to organs at risk (OARs). Physicists update the electron density map to reflect anatomical changes, recalculating the predicted.

plan using original beam fluence and re-optimizing it to meet clinical goals. Plans followed ICRU91 guidelines with an isodose line near 80%. Dose differences between predicted, adapted, and original plans were analyzed for target coverage and OARs. Treatment duration and toxicity were recorded. Survival outcomes were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of 41 patients were enrolled, receiving 232 fractions, of which 178 (76.7%) were treated with ASRT. Online adaptation significantly improved target coverage (median V100% change: +0.1%±2.5%) compared to predicted plans (−2.6%±7.3%, p < 0.001), without significant differences in OAR doses. Median total treatment time was 28 min, with an average 5-minute ASRT workflow. No grade ≥ 3 toxicities were reported; grade 2 events occurred in 10.3% of patients. At a median follow-up of 19.8 months, 1-year local control, disease-free survival, and overall survival for the whole cohort were 94%, 80%, and 84%, respectively.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Daily changes in the body contour and ED heterogeneity can result in major effects on plan dosimetry which can be quickly corrected with ASRT procedure. ASRT is a safe, effective, and time-efficient alternative for online MRIgRT adaptation in thoracic tumours, with promising clinical outcomes and toxicity profiles.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Magnetic Resonance Imaging-guided radiotherapy (MRIgRT) has recently emerged as a transformative technology in the field of radiation oncology, offering several advantages over conventional approaches, such as the superior soft-tissue contrast offered by MRI and the capability for daily adaptation of treatment plans based on patient-specific anatomical changes [1], [2].

Clinical studies have demonstrated that MRIgRT can improve local control in certain treatment sites, such as pancreas, and reduce treatment-related toxicity in others, including prostate, when compared to traditional Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT)-guided radiotherapy [3], [4].

Among the different anatomical regions, the thorax represents a particularly promising site for MRIgRT implementation: the use of MRI-Linac allows real-time tumor motion monitoring through continuous planar MR imaging during treatment, combined with the possibility of on-table daily plan adaptation [5], [6].

Even before the advent of MRI-linacs, stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) had already shown excellent results in the management of pulmonary lesions. In 2010, Timmerman et al. reported a 97.6% three-year local control rate in patients with early-stage NSCLC treated with ablative doses exceeding 100 Gy (biologically effective dose), although grade 3 and 4 adverse events were observed in 12.7% and 3.6% of patients, respectively [7]. Similar findings were confirmed in 2019 in a multicentre phase III trial, where SABR achieved superior freedom from local treatment failure compared with standard radiotherapy (2.6 years vs. 2.1 years), though at the cost of increased toxicity (1 grade 4 and 7 grade 3 events vs. 2 grade 3 events) [7].

The potential of SABR has also been demonstrated in the setting of metastatic pulmonary disease: in a heterogeneous cohort including 43% of lung metastases, Palma et al. reported a one-year local control rate of 75%, with approximately 30% of patients experiencing grade 2 adverse events [8].

Despite these encouraging results, further improvements may be achievable by exploiting the technological potential of MRI-Linac systems: reducing toxicity further, for example by safely shrinking planning target volume (PTV) margins, or increasing treatment efficacy through dose escalation could prolong disease-free intervals and improve outcomes in radioresistant metastases, such as those from colorectal and head and neck cancer, which currently show suboptimal clinical end-points.

Achieving these objectives requires high fidelity in dose accuracy not only at the initial planning stage but also throughout the different treatment fractions: this is particularly critical in the thorax, where high electron density (ED) heterogeneity is present and even small variations in breathing pattern can result in clinically relevant dosimetric deviations.

Online adaptive MRIgRT (MRIgART) is the only strategy capable of providing daily ED updates and recalculations based on the actual anatomy, effectively compensating for inter-fraction variability and ensuring accurate dose delivery over the entire treatment course.

The first application of online MRIgART in the thorax was reported in 2018 in a phase I study of five patients with ultracentral lung lesions treated with MRIdian Cobalt. The study suggested potential dosimetric benefits in PTV coverage, but at the cost of prolonged treatment sessions, with a median duration of 69 min (range 22–117 min) [9]. First clinical outcomes were reported in 2020, when Finazzi et al. showed results from a cohort of 54 high-risk lung cancer patients (including both NSCLC and metastases) treated with online MRIgART. One-year outcomes were promising (95.6% local control, 88% overall survival, 63.6% disease-free survival), with moderate toxicity (30% grade 2, 8% grade 3, no grade 4). However, total treatment times remained substantial, ranging from 41 to 90 min, raising concerns about feasibility and patient comfort [10]. Further clinical evidence supporting the benefits of online adaptive MRIgRT in the thoracic setting was reported in 2023, when Lee et al. observed a one-year local control rate of 96% and a favorable toxicity profile (23% grade 2, 4% grade 3, no grade 4) in a cohort of 26 patients with central and ultracentral oligometastases [11]. In the same year, Sandoval et al. analysed 47 cases of ultracentral lung lesions, reporting a local control rate of 87%, although only 16 patients in the cohort were treated with online MRIgART [12].

The temporal limitations of online MRIgART have been a major concern across all reported experiences, becoming particularly critical in single-fraction treatments, where high doses per fraction further prolong delivery times. In the recently published SMART ONE trial investigating single-fraction MRIgRT treatments, eleven lung lesions were treated and none of these was administered with online adaptation [13].

Since treatment time is a well-recognized barrier in the clinical implementation of online MRIgART, there is an urgent need for more time-efficient adaptive workflows that reserve the main benefits of adaptation while making the process clinically sustainable.

In this context, this study introduces and evaluates a novel online adaptive workflow, termed Adaptive Skin Radiotherapy (ASRT). This minimalist approach is designed to drastically reduce on-table time by rapidly updating only the patient body contour and target volume, while reusing prior organs at risks (OARs) contours whenever feasible. This enables fast correction of the electron density (ED) map to reflect daily anatomical changes and lesion displacement, followed by rapid re-optimization of the original beam fluence.

This prospective study reports the clinical outcomes and dosimetric advantages of this approach, aiming to provide a more sustainable and effective solution for MRIgRT online adaptive in the thoracic setting.

sec.title: Patient selection
sec.p: Patients affected by thoracic malignant lesions, including both primary NSLC tumors and metastatic thoracic disease, were prospectively analysed.

All the patients were treated with breath-hold MRIgRT using the ASRT workflow on the 0.35 T MR-Linac (MRIdian, ViewRay Systems, Oakwood Village, Ohio, US) at Mater Olbia Hospital (Olbia, Sassari, Italy) between January 2023 and December 2024. A BED10 higher or equal to 100 Gy was prescribed to all the patients, with total prescribed doses ranging from 42 to 60 Gy in 3–8 fractions.

The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board. Baseline Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status was recorded for all participants prior to treatment initiation.

Patients were eligible for inclusion if complete imaging, treatment planning, and dosimetric data were available. Exclusion criteria included contraindications to MRI (e.g., non-compatible implants), severe claustrophobia, weight under 50 kg, non-compliance to breath-hold or age under 18 years.

sec.title: Treatment workflow
sec.p: Each patient underwent a dual simulation protocol: the first simulation was performed on the MRIdian system using a dedicated immobilization device (FluxBoard, MacroMedics, The Netherlands) and an audio-visual guidance system. A 25-second 3D MRI scan was acquired using a True Fast Imaging with Steady-State Precession (TrueFISP) sequence under inspiratory breath-hold conditions [14]. Breath-hold compliance was verified via cine-mode acquisition, during which each patient performed three consecutive breath-holds of at least 15 s.

Immediately after MRI simulation, a non-contrast-enhanced CT scan was acquired on the RT Discovery scanner (GE Healthcare, Massachusetts, USA) under the same breath-hold conditions. The simulation CT was deformably registered to the MRI scan and therapy volumes, including Gross Tumour Volume (GTV) and OARs, were delineated on the simulation MRI. Planning Target Volume (PTV) was then generated by applying a 3 mm isotropic margin to the GTV, considering the online adaptation.

Intensity-Modulated Radiotherapy (IMRT) planning was performed using the MRIdian treatment planning system (TPS), employing a Monte Carlo dose calculation algorithm that accounted for the 0.35 T magnetic field from the fluence map generation stage. Plans were generated with a dose calculation grid of 2 mm, using 15 to 24 beams and maintaining the beam-on time under 10 min. Treatment plans were optimized following ICRU Report 91, employing a prescription isodose line ranging between 70 and 90% or ICRU 83 for homogeneous prescription and following 2022 UK consensus dose constraints [15], [16], [17].

sec.title: ASRT workflow
sec.p: The ASRT approach implements a fast and simplified online adaptive workflow, aiming to reduce procedural complexity and accelerate the online adaptation process. After daily MRI acquisition, the body contour within a field of view extending 2 cm in cranio-caudal from the lesion extremities was reviewed by both the radiation oncologist and the medical physicist. If a deviation greater than 2 mm was observed between the daily and original body contour, the ASRT workflow was applied.
At each treatment fraction, only the patient’s body contour was recontoured on the daily MRI, while the GTV and OARs were rigidly propagated from the simulation MRI.

The GTV and the two organs associated with the most common toxicities in thoracic MRIgRT (lung for radiation pneumonitis and chest wall for pain) were visually evaluated by the radiation oncologist and adjusted only in cases of significant variation. The heart, oesophagus, trachea, and bronchial tree were visually assessed only when found within 2 cm from the PTV.
The ED map is generated from the planning CT and subsequently updated by the medical physicist using predefined structures with fixed ED values. Specifically, three bulk-ED structures were employed:

list-item.p: Skin Water: defined as the volume corresponding to the difference between the daily MRI–derived skin contour and the planning CT skin contour with ED set to 1.
Skin Air: defined as the volume corresponding to the difference between the planning CT skin contour and the daily MRI skin contour with ED set to 0.0001.
GTV override: applied only when the propagation of the GTV was inaccurate. In such cases, the GTV ED was set to a bulk value equal to the median GTV ED calculated on the planning CT.

sec.p: The original beam fluence was then recalculated on the daily MRI to generate the so-called “predicted plan”, followed by online re-optimization to obtain the adapted plan. The two plans were compared, and the plan selected for treatment delivery was finally approved by the clinician and underwent independent online quality assurance using a secondary Monte Carlo algorithm.

sec.title: Workflow performance and dosimetric evaluation
sec.p: The performance of the ASRT workflow in terms of time efficiency was evaluated by measuring total treatment time and online ASRT time, measured from the MRI acquisition to final plan approval.
To evaluate the dosimetric impact of the ASRT workflow, predicted and reoptimized plans were compared for each treatment fraction.
Metrics analysed for the PTV included volume covered by the prescription isodose line (Vprescr%), near-minimum (D98%), median (D50%) and near-maximum dose (D2%) [17].
The analysed OARs for all lesions were bronchial tree (D0.1 cc and V16.5 Gy) and chest wall (D0.1 cc and V39 Gy), whereas the D0.1 cc of heart was taken into consideration in case of central lesions.

All contours, covering both OARs and GTV, underwent offline review by a radiation oncologist for each adapted treatment fraction. The statistical significance of observed differences was tested using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test for paired samples, with a significance threshold of p < 0.05 [18].

sec.title: Clinical follow-up and outcome assessment
sec.p: All patients were evaluated for clinical outcomes and treatment-related toxicities: reported toxicities were independently reviewed and confirmed by at least two radiation oncologists and graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE), version 5.0.
Clinical endpoints included LC and OS for all patients included in the study, PFS for metastatic patients, and DFS for NSCLC patients; all were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method [19].

Local control was censored at the date of the last available thoracic imaging. For NSCLC patients, DFS was defined as the interval from the end of radiotherapy to any recurrence. For metastatic cases, PFS was defined as the time from the end of radiotherapy to disease progression at any site.
Local recurrence was determined by a dedicated multidisciplinary team through a validated scoring system based on imaging assessment and biopsy results when available.
Median follow-up was calculated using the reverse Kaplan–Meier method. All statistical analyses were performed using RStudio (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Wien, Austria).

sec.title: Clinical and treatment characteristics
sec.p: A total of 41 patients and 45 lesions were treated, seven of which with early-stage NSCLC and 34 with pulmonary metastases. Clinical characteristics are summarised in Table 1.

caption.p: Clinical characteristics of the patients enrolled in the study: in the table are reported histology, age, ECOG status, risk factor, gender and lesion location.

sec.p: In terms of treatment prescription, two patients with ultra-central tumours were treated with 60 Gy in eight fractions. One patient received 42 Gy in three fractions. The remaining 38 patients were treated with five fractions regimens: four received 55 Gy and 34 received 50 Gy. The median GTV for primary tumors was 3 cc (range: 2.6–40 cc), while the median GTV for metastatic lesions was 2.45 cc (range: 0.3–55.2 cc). Treatment planning was based on ICRU Report 91 in 39 patients and on ICRU Report 83 in 6 patients.

sec.title: Clinical endpoints and toxicity profiles
sec.p: The Kaplan-Meier curve for all the patients included in the study is reported in Fig. 1.

caption.p: Kaplan-Meier curve for all the patients included in the study: in red PFS/DFS, in green LC and in blue OS. (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.)

sec.p: The median follow-up was 19.8 months (95% CI: 18.0–23.9 months). After one year from the end of the RT treatment, local control was 94% (95% CI: 86%–100%), DFS/PFS was 80% (95% CI: 67%–96%), and OS was 84% (95% CI: 73%–98%) in the overall study cohort. All local failures occurred in the metastatic setting, with one failure from NSCLC metastases and one from head and neck. Excluding the seven NSCLC patients and focusing only on the metastatic setting, at one year LC was 92% (95% CI: 83%–100%), PFS was 74% (95% CI: 59%–94%), and OS was 81% (95% CI: 67%–98%).

At the time of analysis, 8 patients had died. The most common cause of death was cardiovascular disease (4 cases); one patient died of immune-mediated bilateral pneumonitis, two patients from aspiration pneumonia, and in one case the cause of death was unknown. For the patient who died from pneumonitis, a contribution of SBRT can be ruled out, as immunotherapy was initiated 13 months after the end of radiotherapy.

Toxicity data were available for 39 of 41 patients. No grade 3 or higher toxicities were reported. A total of four grade 2 (G2) adverse events (10.3%) were observed: two cases of oesophagitis, one case of fatigue, and one case of radiation pneumonitis. The patient who developed radiation pneumonitis had previously received thoracic radiotherapy. Additionally, 13 grade 1 toxicity events were recorded. The most common was fatigue (n = 9), followed by chest wall pain (n = 3) and one case of lung infection.

sec.title: Treatment characteristics and dose analysis
sec.p: A total of 178 out of 232 fractions (76.7%) were delivered using the online ASRT protocol. Manual adjustment of the GTV was required in five fractions only (2.8%), while adjustment of OARs was needed in 21 out of 178 fractions (11.7%).

Offline re–evaluation was performed for all ASRT fractions. No modifications to the GTV were required in any of the reviewed fractions. Overall, five fractions (2.8%) required minor adjustments: two involving the bronchial tree (1.1%) and three involving the chest wall (1.7%).

Fig. 2 illustrates a boxplot showing the relative percentage difference between the predicted and adapted plans compared to the original plan, across all adapted fractions and patients in the cohort. The comparison focused on the volume of the prescription dose covering the PTV (V100%) and the main dose values describing dose distribution within PTV (D2%, D50%, D98%).

caption.p: Boxplot showing the differences from the original plan for each treatment fraction, comparing the adapted (Adp) and predicted (Pred) plans. Percentage target coverage V100% is reported in top, percentage dose difference in terms of D2%, D98% and D50% of PTV are reported in bottom graph.

sec.p: Without online adaptation, a median reduction with respect the original plan in V100% of −2.6%±7.3% (range: −43.7% to + 3.3%, Interquartile (IQR): 6.5%) was observed. Online plan adaptation led to a statistically significant improvement (p < 0.001), with a median V100% improvement of 0.1% ± 2.5% (range: −13.7% to + 2.7%, IQR: 9.8%).

Regarding PTV dose metrics, the predicted plans without adaptation showed significant variation: D98% ranged from –32% to + 8.7% (IQR: 4.4%), D2% from −26.5% to + 51.5% (IQR: 4.9%), and D50% from −26.8% to + 12.0% (IQR: 3.1%). These variations were markedly reduced with online adaptation, narrowing the ranges to −13.7% to + 3.9% for D98% (IQR:1.6%), −9.4% to + 3.2% for D2% (IQR:2.4%), and −9.1% to + 3.6% for D50% (IQR:1.4%). A significant improvement with online adaptation was observed in D2% and D98% of the PTV (p < 0.001), while no significant difference was found for D50% (p = 0.64).

Analysis of target coverage in the predicted plans revealed that omitting adaptive planning would have led to a coverage loss of less than 5% in 122 out of 178 cases (68.5%), between 5% and 10% in 24 cases (13.5%), and greater than 10% in 31 cases (18%). Regarding OARs, no significant benefit from adaptive planning was observed when considering the entire cohort. However, in the subgroup of central and ultra central lesions, the ASRT approach resulted in a significant improvement in the reduction of D0.1 cc of the bronchial tree (p = 0.039).

Regarding treatment delivery, the average total time for the ASRT workflow was 28 min, ranging from 25 to 50 min. Focusing specifically on the ASRT workflow, the on-table manual procedures −including contouring, ED check and planning − took on average 5 min (range: 2–9 min). The distribution of the different component of the treatment times is illustrated in Fig. 3.

caption.p: Box-plot analysis of the main steps of the ASRT workflow.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The thorax is a treatment site where Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy (SBRT) has already shown excellent tumour control outcomes – with 1 year local control rates exceeding 95% in NSCLC and approaching 90% in the metastatic disease, even without MRI-guidance, breath-hold techniques, or online adaptation [7], [8].

Given the already excellent disease control outcomes, the added value of online MRIgART in thoracic tumours likely lies in two areas: improving local control in metastatic disease through precise dose delivery and escalation strategies, and reducing treatment toxicity by enabling smaller treatment volumes and tighter dose conformity [20].

Online adaptation is crucial to ensure robust dose calculation, thereby allowing safe dose escalation and PTV margins reduction. Dose escalation strategies are currently being investigated in ongoing clinical trials, such as the phase I MAGELLAN trial for ultra centrally located lesions and the PUMA trial, where weekly adaptation compensates for tumour shrinkage in longer treatment courses [21], [22].

Time remains the main barrier to the clinical implementation of online MRIgART in the thorax; therefore, ASRT may offer a time-efficient alternative to ensure accurate dose calculation and further enhance treatment quality in lung cancer patients. In this study, local control outcomes observed using ASRT were encouraging, with a 1-year LC rate of 94% for the entire cohort, closely aligning with the findings by Finazzi et al, who reported 95.4% 1-year LC in the largest MRIgRT cohort published to date (n = 54) [10].

Among other clinical endpoints, the one‑year PFS rate observed in this metastatic setting appears favourable, reaching 74%, although this result should be interpreted with caution given the small size of the metastatic cohort (n = 34). Although this value is higher than what is typically reported in MRIgRT and SBRT cohorts [8], [10], differences in patient characteristics and treatment pathways may account for this variability.

Our dosimetric analysis confirmed the benefit of the ASRT approach in improving target coverage. Adaptive plans lead to a significant improvement in V100%, D2% and D98% of PTV, allowing more accurate dose delivery. Comparable findings were reported by Regnery et al., who observed that 94% of fractions did not meet planning objectives without online adaptation [23]. It is noteworthy that the substantial dosimetric variations observed between adapted and predicted plans were calculated after performing the couch shift and are therefore attributable exclusively to inter‑fraction ED variability encountered by the IMRT beams across treatment days.

Importantly, our fast and simplified adaptive approach reached the same local control rates observed by Finazzi et al. with the traditional online adaptive, while reducing the on-table procedure time by approximately 60% (6 vs. 16 min, excluding positioning and beam delivery) [10].

A significant improvement was also observed with respect to the experience of Regnery et al, who reported 14.8 ± 6.9 min for manual recontouring: continued follow-up will be essential to assess whether these dosimetric and workflow improvements translate into long-term clinical benefits[23].

Toxicity is another critical endpoint, with grade ≥ 3 adverse events occurring in a substantial proportion of patients in major studies: 12.7% in Timmerman et al. and 8% in the adaptive high risk MRIgRT cohort of Finazzi et al.). Notably, no grade ≥ 3 toxicity was observed in our cohort, and the incidence of grade 2 events was limited to 10%, lower than the ∼ 30% typically reported in both SBRT and MRIgART setting [7], [10]. Differences in toxicity rates may partially reflect patient-specific risk factors. Compared to Finazzi’s cohort, our patients had lower rates of prior lung RT (12% vs. 34%), coexisting ILD (5% vs 14%) and prior surgery (14% vs. 26%).

A contributing factor might be the use of smaller margins (3 mm vs. 5 mm), which likely limited exposure to healthy lung, along with the shorter treatment duration of the fast adaptive workflow, potentially reducing patient discomfort and fatigue. Unlike treatments in the abdominal region, where the OARs proximity to the target typically drives online adaptation, in the thoracic setting the main rationale for online adaptation lies in ED daily variation.
Partial target miss may lead to unintended high-dose delivery to healthy lung tissue, with doses increasing by up to 12.6 Gy (+25.2%) due to the presence of a different local ED distribution.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In conclusion, ASRT emerges as a safe and efficient technique that significantly reduces treatment time, potentially improving the accessibility of MRIgART in clinical practice. Our results suggest promising outcomes in terms of both tumour control and toxicity, particularly in the thoracic setting, where accurate ED modelling is essential due to the dose perturbations introduced by the magnetic field. Fast simplified adaptation may offer a practical alternative to full adaptation, with the potential to enable safer dose escalation in radioresistant metastases and to minimize treatment-related toxicity. While these findings are encouraging, further validation through larger, multi-center studies with extended follow-up are warranted to fully establish the clinical value of this approach.
